summary: Describes an RTP payload format for H.264 video, excluding the scalable and multiview extensions, which allows packetizing NAL units for network transport. It obsoletes RFC 3984 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6184 explains how to send H.264 video over RTP, the transport used for real-time media. It covers three ways of packing video data into packets, and adds a number that lets the receiver put the pieces back in the right order even when they arrive out of order.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for h.264
what is fu-a fragmentation in rtp
subtitle: How to carry H.264 video over RTP, including how to split large frames and put small ones together.

tldr.problem: H.264 encoders produce blocks of video data that rarely match the size of a network packet, and some blocks are far too big to fit in one. A video call also needs the receiver to rebuild the picture in the right order.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how those blocks, called NAL units, are carried in RTP packets: one per packet, several packed together, or a large one split across packets. A decoding order number tells the receiver which order to feed the blocks to the decoder.
tldr.outcome: The RFC obsoletes RFC 3984 and adds the interleaved mode, the decoding order number and several SDP parameters. It excludes the scalable and multiview extensions, which have their own payload formats.

facts.label: Largest NAL unit in an aggregation

today: RFC 6184 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3984; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Payload Format Does
sections.content:
The memo specifies an RTP payload format for the ITU-T Recommendation H.264 video codec and the technically identical ISO/IEC International Standard 14496-10, excluding the Scalable Video Coding and Multiview Video Coding extensions, for which the payload formats are defined elsewhere. It allows one or more Network Abstraction Layer Units produced by an H.264 encoder to be packetized in each RTP payload, and it has wide applicability, from simple low bitrate conversational use to Internet video streaming with interleaved transmission and high bitrate video on demand.

The H.264 codec specification conceptually distinguishes a Video Coding Layer and a Network Abstraction Layer. The coding layer holds the signal processing: transform, quantization, motion-compensated prediction and a loop filter. It outputs slices, which are bit strings carrying the macroblock data of an integer number of macroblocks plus a slice header. The network abstraction layer encapsulates those slices into NAL units, which are suitable for transmission over packet networks. A NAL unit consists of a one-byte header and a payload byte string, where the header indicates the type of the unit, the possible presence of bit errors, and the unit's relative importance to the decoding process. This payload specification is designed to be unaware of the bit string inside the NAL unit payload.

One of the main properties of H.264 is the complete decoupling of transmission time, decoding time and sampling or presentation time. A related design idea is the parameter set: information relevant to more than one slice, such as picture size and the coding modes in use, is pulled out of the media stream so that the slices become self-contained. The sequence parameter set stays unchanged through a coded video sequence and the picture parameter set within a coded picture, and an encoder may keep several of each so that a change of picture size does not require synchronising a parameter set update with the slice stream. The parameter sets are normally sent reliably, asynchronously and in advance of the RTP stream, though in-band transport is also possible.
sections.plainLanguage: An H.264 encoder produces slices of video data. This document says how to put those slices into RTP packets so that a receiver can rebuild the picture. The settings that describe the video, such as its size, travel separately from the slices.

sections.title: The Three Payload Structures
sections.content:
The payload format defines three basic payload structures. A receiver identifies which one is present from the first byte of the RTP payload, which always co-serves as the RTP payload header and in some cases as the first byte of the payload. That byte is always structured as a NAL unit header, and its type field says which structure follows.

A single NAL unit packet contains only a single NAL unit, with the NAL header type field equal to the original NAL unit type, in the range 1 to 23. An aggregation packet packs multiple NAL units into one RTP payload, and exists in four versions: the Single-Time Aggregation Packet type A, STAP-A; the Single-Time Aggregation Packet type B, STAP-B; the Multi-Time Aggregation Packet with a 16-bit offset, MTAP16; and the Multi-Time Aggregation Packet with a 24-bit offset, MTAP24. Their NAL unit type numbers are 24, 25, 26 and 27. A fragmentation unit splits a single NAL unit over multiple RTP packets, and exists in two versions, FU-A and FU-B, identified by NAL unit type numbers 28 and 29. NAL unit type 0 and types 30 to 31 are reserved.

The aggregation scheme exists because the two target networks have very different packet sizes: wireline IP networks, where the MTU is often limited by the Ethernet MTU of roughly 1500 bytes, and wireless systems using IP or ITU-T H.324/M, with preferred transmission unit sizes of 254 bytes or less. Rather than transcode between the two worlds, the sender aggregates. The specification does not limit the size of NAL units carried in single NAL unit packets and fragmentation units, but the maximum size of a NAL unit encapsulated in any aggregation packet is 65535 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet starts with a byte that says what kind of packet it is. The three kinds are: one block of video on its own, several blocks packed together, or one block split across several packets.

sections.title: The NAL Unit Header
sections.content:
The NAL unit type octet carries three fields. The F bit, one bit, is the forbidden_zero_bit. A value of 0 indicates that the NAL unit type octet and payload should not contain bit errors or other syntax violations, while a value of 1 indicates that they may. The H.264 specification itself requires the F bit to be 0. Media-aware network elements SHOULD set the F bit to indicate detected bit errors, and the simplest decoder reaction to a NAL unit whose F bit is 1 is to discard it and conceal the lost data.

The NRI field, two bits, is the nal_ref_idc. A value of 00 indicates that the content of the NAL unit is not used to reconstruct reference pictures for inter picture prediction, so such NAL units can be discarded without risking the integrity of the reference pictures. Values greater than 00 indicate that decoding the NAL unit is required to maintain the integrity of the reference pictures. The Type field, five bits, specifies the NAL unit payload type as defined in the H.264 specification.

The memo introduces new NAL unit types, marked as unspecified in the H.264 specification, and extends the semantics of the F and NRI bits. It also notes that the RTP payload type assignment for the new packet format is out of scope and must be done through the profile used or dynamically. The marker bit in the RTP header is set on the very last packet of an access unit. For aggregation packets the marker bit MUST be set to the value it would have had for the last NAL unit of the aggregation packet had it been transported on its own, and decoders MAY use it as an early indication but MUST NOT rely on it. The RTP timestamp is set to the sampling timestamp of the content, and a 90 kHz clock rate MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The header byte says three things: whether the data may be damaged, how important the block is to the decoder, and what kind of block it is. The timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock.

sections.title: The Three Packetization Modes
sections.content:
The memo specifies three packetization modes. Single NAL unit mode is targeted at conversational systems that comply with ITU-T Recommendation H.241. Non-interleaved mode is targeted at conversational systems that may not comply with H.241; in this mode NAL units are transmitted in NAL unit decoding order. Interleaved mode is targeted at systems that do not require very low end-to-end latency and allows NAL units to be transmitted out of decoding order. The mode in use MAY be signalled by the value of the optional packetization-mode media type parameter.

Single NAL unit mode is in use when the packetization-mode parameter is 0 or absent. All receivers MUST support it. It is intended for low-delay applications, only single NAL unit packets MAY be used, and STAPs, MTAPs and FUs MUST NOT be used. Non-interleaved mode is in use when the parameter is 1 and SHOULD be supported; only single NAL unit packets, STAP-As and FU-As MAY be used, and the transmission order MUST comply with the NAL unit decoding order. Interleaved mode is in use when the parameter is 2 and some receivers MAY support it; STAP-Bs, MTAPs, FU-As and FU-Bs MAY be used, while STAP-As and single NAL unit packets MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Three modes trade simplicity against flexibility. The simplest allows only one block per packet. The middle one also allows packing and splitting, but keeps everything in order. The most flexible one lets packets travel out of order, which helps when latency matters less than robustness.

sections.title: The Decoding Order Number
sections.content:
In the interleaved packetization mode the transmission order of NAL units is allowed to differ from their decoding order. The decoding order number, DON, is a field in the payload structure or a derived variable that indicates the NAL unit decoding order. The coupling of transmission and decoding order is controlled by the optional sprop-interleaving-depth media type parameter: when it is 0, explicitly or by default, the transmission order of NAL units MUST conform to the NAL unit decoding order; when it is greater than 0, the order of NAL units inside an MTAP16 or MTAP24 is not required to be the decoding order, and neither is the order produced by de-packetizing STAP-Bs, MTAPs and FUs in two consecutive packets.

The payload structures for a single NAL unit packet, an STAP-A and an FU-A do not include the DON. The STAP-B and FU-B structures include it, and the structure of the MTAPs enables it to be derived. Values of DON are in the range 0 to 65535, inclusive, and after reaching the maximum value the value wraps around to 0. The decoding order of two NAL units carried in an STAP-B, an MTAP, or a series of fragmentation units starting with an FU-B is determined by a function that compares two DON values and takes into account the wrap-around, with the difference of 32768 as the decision point. A positive result means the second NAL unit follows the first in decoding order, a negative result means it precedes, and zero means either order is acceptable.

Two NAL units whose order in decoding order is switched MUST NOT have the same DON value if the new order does not conform to the NAL unit decoding order. When the order is switched and the new order still conforms, they MAY share a DON value. For example, when the video coding profile in use allows arbitrary slice order, all the coded slice NAL units of a coded picture may have the same DON value, and NAL units with the same DON value can be decoded in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: In the most flexible mode, packets may arrive in a different order from the one the decoder needs. Each block carries a number that says where it belongs, so the receiver can sort them before decoding.

sections.title: Fragmenting a NAL Unit
sections.content:
A fragmentation unit splits one NAL unit across several RTP packets. Doing this on the application layer rather than relying on lower-layer fragmentation has two advantages: it can carry NAL units bigger than 64 kbytes over an IPv4 network, which matters for pre-recorded video in high-definition formats, and it lets a single NAL unit be fragmented and protected with generic forward error correction.

Fragmentation is defined only for a single NAL unit and not for aggregation packets. A fragment is an integer number of consecutive octets of that NAL unit, and each octet MUST be part of exactly one fragment. Fragments of the same NAL unit MUST be sent in consecutive order with ascending RTP sequence numbers, and a NAL unit MUST be reassembled in sequence number order. STAPs and MTAPs MUST NOT be fragmented, and fragmentation units MUST NOT be nested.

An FU-A consists of a one-octet fragmentation unit indicator, a one-octet fragmentation unit header and a fragmentation unit payload. An FU-B adds a decoding order number field in network byte order. The indicator octet has the same F, NRI and Type layout as a NAL unit header, and its type value of 28 identifies an FU-A and 29 an FU-B; the NRI field MUST be set according to the NRI field of the fragmented NAL unit. The FU header carries a Start bit, an End bit, a Reserved bit that MUST be 0 and MUST be ignored by the receiver, and the 5-bit NAL unit type. A fragmented NAL unit MUST NOT be transmitted in one FU, so the Start bit and End bit MUST NOT both be set in the same FU header. The NAL unit type octet of the fragmented NAL unit is not repeated in the payload; its information is carried in the indicator and header instead. If a fragmentation unit is lost, the receiver SHOULD discard all the following fragmentation units for the same fragmented NAL unit.
sections.plainLanguage: When one block is too big for a packet, it is cut into pieces. Each piece carries a flag saying whether it is the first, the last, or one in between, so the receiver can glue them back together and can tell when one is missing.

sections.title: Signalling the Format with SDP
sections.content:
The media type video/H264 string maps to fields of the Session Description Protocol. The media name in the m= line MUST be video, the encoding name in the a=rtpmap line MUST be H264, and the clock rate in the a=rtpmap line MUST be 90000. Optional parameters, when present, MUST be included in the a=fmtp line as a semicolon-separated list of parameter=value pairs. The parameters include profile-level-id, max-recv-level, max-mbps, max-smbps, max-fs, max-cpb, max-dpb, max-br, redundant-pic-cap, use-level-src-parameter-sets, in-band-parameter-sets, level-asymmetry-allowed, packetization-mode, sprop-interleaving-depth, sprop-deint-buf-req, deint-buf-cap, sprop-init-buf-time, sprop-max-don-diff, max-rcmd-nalu-size, sar-understood and sar-supported.

The parameters sprop-parameter-sets and sprop-level-parameter-sets, when present, MUST be included in the a=fmtp line or conveyed using the fmtp source attribute. For a particular media format, the two MUST NOT both be included in the a=fmtp line and conveyed using the fmtp source attribute. An example of media representation in SDP is m=video 49170 RTP/AVP 98, a=rtpmap:98 H264/90000 and an a=fmtp line with profile-level-id, packetization-mode and sprop-parameter-sets.

In the SDP offer/answer model, the parameters that identify a media format configuration are profile-level-id and packetization-mode, and these MUST be used symmetrically, except for the level part of profile-level-id. The answerer MUST either maintain all configuration parameters or remove the media format completely if one or more parameter values are not supported. The same RTP payload type number used in the offer SHOULD also be used in the answer, and an answer MUST NOT contain the payload type number used in the offer unless the configuration is exactly the same. Compared with RFC 3984, the memo makes clear that the level is downgradable, so the level in the answer may be lower than or equal to the level in the offer, and it adds the parameters max-recv-level and level-asymmetry-allowed for level upgrade and asymmetry.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree on the format before the call starts, using the same kind of description that web and streaming systems use. The clock rate is fixed at 90 kHz, and the answer must offer the same configuration or drop the format entirely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and of any applicable RTP profile. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption, for example through SRTP. Because the data compression used with this payload format is applied end to end, any encryption needs to be performed after compression.

A potential denial-of-service threat exists for data encodings using compression techniques that have non-uniform receiver-end computational load: an attacker can inject pathological datagrams that are complex to decode and that overload the receiver. H.264 is particularly vulnerable to such attacks, because it is extremely simple to generate datagrams containing NAL units that affect the decoding process of many future NAL units. The usage of data origin authentication and data integrity protection of at least the RTP packet is therefore RECOMMENDED, for example with SRTP.

Decoders MUST exercise caution with respect to the handling of user data SEI messages, particularly if they contain active elements, and MUST restrict their domain of applicability to the presentation containing the stream. End-to-end security with authentication, integrity or confidentiality protection will prevent a media-aware network element from performing media-aware operations other than discarding complete packets; with confidentiality protection it will even be prevented from discarding packets in a media-aware way. To be allowed to perform its operations, a media-aware network element has to be a trusted entity included in the security context establishment. Congestion control follows RTP, and users of this payload format MUST monitor packet loss so that the loss rate stays within acceptable parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the video is what protects the call, but it also stops a router in the middle from dropping the least useful packets. The format is also easy to attack with data that is expensive to decode, so the RFC recommends authenticating the packets.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forbidden zero bit. Set to 1 to signal that bit errors or syntax violations may be present.

fields.name: NRI
fields.desc: nal_ref_idc. A value of 00 means the unit is not needed to rebuild reference pictures.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: nal_unit_type. Also says which RTP payload structure the packet uses.

viz.caption: NAL UNIT TYPES AND THE PACKET TYPE EACH ONE MEANS

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Not used and to be ignored by receivers.

items.label: STAP-A
items.desc: Single-time aggregation packet, without a decoding order number.

items.label: STAP-B
items.desc: Single-time aggregation packet, with a decoding order number.

items.label: MTAP16
items.desc: Multi-time aggregation packet with a 16-bit timestamp offset.

items.label: MTAP24
items.desc: Multi-time aggregation packet with a 24-bit timestamp offset.

items.label: FU-B
items.desc: Fragmentation unit, with a decoding order number.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Not used and to be ignored by receivers.
